Frequently asked questions

Five questions to understand the Ishango bone. Read, explore and check what you learned.

1

When did it happen?

About 20,000 years ago, in the Upper Palaeolithic (Stone Age). Humanity had neither writing nor agriculture then, and for a long time it was assumed that people did not practise abstract thought either.

The Ishango bone challenges that assumption: its marks are ordered in groups and were carved thousands of years before agriculture and writing.

Tap or hover a milestone.

Approximate dates.

2

Where did it happen?

In central Africa: at Ishango, on the shore of Lake Edward, in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo, next to the border with Uganda.

It was not in Greece or in Europe. Marks ordered in groups appear in Africa about 17,000 years before the first Greek mathematicians. Recognising this corrects a Eurocentric view of where mathematical thinking began.

3

What is it?

It is the fibula —a long bone of the leg— of a baboon, about 10 cm long. It carries 168 carved marks in 3 columns and, at one end, a small fragment of quartz (the white tip visible in the photograph), perhaps used for engraving.

4

What is a notch? How was it made?

A notch is a small cut made on the edge or surface of an object; it is also called a mark or a score. To carve is to shape a material by removing parts of it.

At Ishango the marks were made by scratching the bone with a sharp stone point. Each scratch counts one unit, and the scratches are gathered into 16 groups.

5

What is it good for? What is a prime? And a twin prime?

A prime number

A prime number is greater than 1 and is divisible only by 1 and itself: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13… All other numbers, the composites, are built by multiplying primes, which is why primes are called the “atoms” of numbers.

A twin prime

Two primes are twins if they differ by 2: (3, 5), (5, 7), (11, 13), (17, 19)… Nobody yet knows whether there are infinitely many such pairs.

What are primes for?

Digital security

Multiplying two huge primes is easy; recovering the two primes from the result is extremely hard. Much of the cryptography that protects payments and messages relies on that asymmetry.

Foundation of arithmetic

Every integer greater than 1 can be written in exactly one way as a product of primes (the fundamental theorem of arithmetic).

Nature

Some North American cicadas emerge every 13 or 17 years, both primes, which is thought to reduce overlap with predators and with other broods.

Computing

They are used in hash tables, pseudo-random generators and error-correcting codes.

6

Test what you learned

Five quick questions, one per topic. Unlimited attempts.

Roughly how many years ago was the bone carved?

About 20,000 years ago, in the Upper Palaeolithic, before agriculture and writing.

Where was it found?

At Ishango, on the shore of Lake Edward, in today’s DR Congo: not in Greece or Europe.

Which animal does the bone come from?

It is the fibula of a baboon and measures about 10 cm.

How were the notches made?

The bone was scratched with a stone point; a fragment of quartz survives at one end.

Which of these pairs are twin primes?

11 and 13 are prime and differ by 2. 9 is not prime (3 × 3).
